How I build a sandcastle

It all seems fairly simple, really: scoop some wet sand into a bucket, flip the bucket over, give the bottom a firm tap with your hand (or a little shovel, if you want to be fancy about it), and ta-da! You've got yourself a sandcastle. Mine's the lopsided one over on the left, in case you were wondering.

How do other people build a sandcastle?

Clearly, some people take sandcastle building far more seriously than I do. These people know a thing or two about sand! Sand grains vary quite a bit in size, but technically speaking, to actually count as sand, a particle has to measure between 0.0625 mm and 2 mm across. Anything bigger than that is a pebble or a small rock, not sand at all. Professional sand sculptors use sand with square-edged grains, since this type of sand, when packed down while very damp, can be carved and shaped into genuinely amazing structures. For those of us who don't bring a microscope to the beach to inspect grain shape, the real trick, according to the experts, is simply to use very wet sand - it holds its shape far better.

A short history of sand

Sand is created when rocks, coral and shells are gradually broken down into tiny fragments by the constant action of wind and water. These fragments get carried along by wind or washed down rivers into the ocean. Looking at individual grains of sand under a microscope can actually reveal a surprising amount about where they came from. Quartz sand that has broken down from granite, for example, tends to have sharp, angular edges, while sand that has travelled a long way usually ends up rounder and smoother. The sand on your local beach has probably spent thousands of years tumbling around in the ocean, which is why it's usually fairly rounded. This matters for serious sandcastle builders: larger grains don't stick together easily, and rounded grains don't hold together nearly as well as sharper, more angular ones do.

In her own words

My teacher says
I write beautiful stories.
Essays too. He loves
reading my work.
But he doesn't understand my poems.

Ha, I think to myself.
What would he know?
I love writing poems.
He wants
rhyme and rhythm
and neat, happy endings

but my poems
don't rhyme,
can't rhyme,
shouldn't rhyme.

Rhyme
isn't what makes a poem.

Dad makes a small sound
of surprise.
He didn't know
his daughter wrote poems.
I never show him my notebooks.
I never showed my grandpa either.

Wrong, Dad!
Grandpa knew.

On slow afternoons
when you were at work
and Grandpa and I
had the house to ourselves,

I would read him my poems
and he would read me his.

One afternoon
Grandpa read me
a poem
about a fox stealing an egg.

Grandpa, I asked him,
why doesn't this poem rhyme?

Grandpa laughed.

Why, Amira, he said,
didn't you know
a poem doesn't have to rhyme?
It doesn't have to look
a certain way,
follow a certain rule.

No.
A poem arrives
exactly when it's needed
and writes itself
in whatever shape
it needs
to say what it means.

A day at the reptile park

This is an extract from the novel The Curious Case of Nadia Finch, by Priya Talwar.

Sister Constance is the name Nadia and Farhan have secretly given to the strict nun who supervises them at St Aloysius School.

Ordinarily, Nadia and Farhan would have sat as far away as physically possible from Sister Constance. If the nun took a seat at the front of the bus, they'd happily have squeezed in right at the back, practically in a different postcode. But today was different - today, they needed to be close to the action.

Their eyes were fixed on Sister Constance's built-up shoe, and the faint clicking sound it made with every step. Nadia was thrilled that her theory about the shoe had finally been confirmed. The only question now was how long it would take to find out exactly what was hidden inside it.

The clicking might stop suddenly, or it might carry on for the whole excursion - there was no way to know for certain. Both girls agreed to keep a close eye on things; it might take a while.

In the meantime, Nadia was determined to actually enjoy her day at the reptile park.

They arrived, and Sister Constance clapped her hands sharply and herded the class into two straight lines. Blowing a shrill whistle, she marched at the very front of the group. She'd deliberately separated Nadia and Farhan to stop them whispering and giggling together. These two, she'd decided, had an irritating habit of enjoying themselves far too much, and she wasn't going to allow that kind of nonsense in her class - it needed to be stamped out entirely.

But it would take more than a bit of hand-clapping and whistle-blowing to stop Nadia from having fun. She wanted to wander freely and look at all the different reptiles on display. Sister Constance, however, had the whole day planned down to the last detail, and marched everyone straight towards the crocodile enclosure.

Nadia had no interest in that at all, and as the group rounded a corner, she slipped behind a large potted fern. Turning around, she found herself face to face with a lizard peering back at her through the glass of its tank.

Swimming at the beach is about to feel a little creepier. Hidden in the shallow water of your local beach, and crawling through the coldest, deepest oceans on Earth, are sea spiders - strange, spindly creatures that look like they escaped from a science-fiction film. They range enormously in size, from less than a centimetre across to larger than a dinner plate, and with their tiny bodies and impossibly long legs, they're easy to imagine crawling all over you. But it gets stranger still.

Sea spiders feed using a long tube-like mouthpart called a proboscis, which they poke directly into the soft body of their prey before sucking out its insides. Surprisingly, many of these unlucky victims survive this gruesome attack. This is partly because the animals sea spiders usually prey on, such as sea sponges and sea anemones, tend to be considerably larger than the sea spider itself - so they can usually recover, at least most of the time.

Their bodies are so thin and simple that they don't need lungs or gills at all - oxygen simply passes straight through their skin in a process called diffusion. In fact, their bodies are so small that many of their internal organs actually extend out into their legs instead. Many sea spiders living deep in the ocean have no need for eyes at all, and are completely blind.

Sea spiders puzzle scientists trying to classify them. They are not true spiders, since true spiders and other arachnids belong to a different animal group entirely. Instead, sea spiders have a hard, segmented outer shell, which places them among the arthropods - the same broad group as insects, crabs and true spiders. Their strange proboscis, though, makes it hard for scientists to agree on exactly where they fit within that group.

Marine biologist Dr Elena Brooks has spent years studying sea spiders, particularly the ones living in the icy waters of Antarctica. 'The Antarctic species tend to be bigger, stranger and far more varied than sea spiders found anywhere else on the planet - that's what makes them so fascinating to study,' she explains.

The Lookout Tower

The year is 3020. The location is a quiet street in a small town called Millbrook.

'Is everyone here?' bellowed Tobias, our self-appointed captain, straightening his recently-inherited cape as he spoke. Six voices mumbled agreement, and someone asked, 'Is this a birthday party?'

'No jokes during a mission briefing,' Tobias tried to boom again, fumbling with the clasp of his cape, which kept threatening to strangle him.

'Today's mission is to build a lookout tower so we can watch for the new kids moving in next door,' Tobias announced.

'We could use some old crates stacked on top of each other,' I suggested.

'That's a terrible idea, Priya,' Tobias declared. Clearly, encouragement was not a skill Tobias had yet developed.

'We'll build it using bricks,' Tobias stated.

'Yes, Tobias. Whatever you say, Tobias,' we all chorused.

All afternoon we hauled bricks, stacking and wedging them until we had a tower that looked as though it had been designed by a toddler with a grudge. Still, it seemed sturdy enough. The last task of the day involved rolling one particularly large brick towards the tower's base, to use as Tobias's own personal podium for future announcements.

The events that followed are recorded in our (extremely secret) mission log, as follows:
1. After a gentle push, the brick gathered speed down a slight slope.
2. The brick rolled onwards (rapidly) towards the tower.
3. The brick struck the tower's foundation, and the foundation shifted.
4. The bricks above tumbled outward like dominoes, flattening Mr Yorke's prize-winning tomato stakes.
5. Without a word to each other, we all fled the scene immediately. Tobias somehow had a head start on the rest of us.

Weeks later, I overheard my mother talking to Mr Yorke about the disaster. 'It must have been that freak gust of wind we had that afternoon,' Mr Yorke insisted loudly. I recognised the voice - it was Tobias's own father. The other parents nodded along sympathetically. Tobias must get his gift for confident leadership from his father, I decided, since neither of them let the facts get in the way of a good story.

The Lookout Tower

The year is 3020. The location is a quiet street in a small town called Millbrook.

'Is everyone here?' bellowed Tobias, our self-appointed captain, straightening his recently-inherited cape as he spoke. Six voices mumbled agreement, and someone asked, 'Is this a birthday party?'

'No jokes during a mission briefing,' Tobias tried to boom again, fumbling with the clasp of his cape, which kept threatening to strangle him.

'Today's mission is to build a lookout tower so we can watch for the new kids moving in next door,' Tobias announced.

'We could use some old crates stacked on top of each other,' I suggested.

'That's a terrible idea, Priya,' Tobias declared. Clearly, encouragement was not a skill Tobias had yet developed.

'We'll build it using bricks,' Tobias stated.

'Yes, Tobias. Whatever you say, Tobias,' we all chorused.

All afternoon we hauled bricks, stacking and wedging them until we had a tower that looked as though it had been designed by a toddler with a grudge. Still, it seemed sturdy enough. The last task of the day involved rolling one particularly large brick towards the tower's base, to use as Tobias's own personal podium for future announcements.

The events that followed are recorded in our (extremely secret) mission log, as follows:
1. After a gentle push, the brick gathered speed down a slight slope.
2. The brick rolled onwards (rapidly) towards the tower.
3. The brick struck the tower's foundation, and the foundation shifted.
4. The bricks above tumbled outward like dominoes, flattening Mr Yorke's prize-winning tomato stakes.
5. Without a word to each other, we all fled the scene immediately. Tobias somehow had a head start on the rest of us.

Weeks later, I overheard my mother talking to Mr Yorke about the disaster. 'It must have been that freak gust of wind we had that afternoon,' Mr Yorke insisted loudly. I recognised the voice - it was Tobias's own father. The other parents nodded along sympathetically. Tobias must get his gift for confident leadership from his father, I decided, since neither of them let the facts get in the way of a good story.

The Daily Journal
Letters to the editor

Thunderdrop
15 September

I rode the new Thunderdrop that Marcus Webb complained about in his letter to your newspaper (Letters, 12 September). It was every bit as 'fast and jarring' as Mr Webb described - which, frankly, is exactly what a theme park ride is supposed to be!

I suspect Mr Webb's real problem is that this ride was unlike anything he'd experienced before. It's fairly obvious he hasn't set foot in a theme park for a very long time. In a way, I understand the complaint: a hundred and fifty years ago, a horse-drawn carousel seemed thrilling, and people were nervous of anything that spun too fast. When the first roller coasters appeared in the early 1900s, they caused a genuine sensation. For Mr Webb, Thunderdrop is simply the modern equivalent - a little frightening, because it's unfamiliar.

Of course, times have changed. Old-fashioned carousels are considered tame now, and if you climb aboard a drop ride, you should expect your stomach to lurch. Carousels are for toddlers, grandparents and the faint-hearted - the Marcus Webbs of the world. Not for me, though.

This is exactly why Mr Webb's claim that something is wrong with Thunderdrop completely misses the point. He was frightened - 'terrified out of my wits' were his exact words. He went on an extreme drop ride and, unsurprisingly, felt extreme. That doesn't mean the ride is faulty or unsafe - it's meant to feel intense. That's how it was built, how it was advertised, and exactly how people my age (myself included) like it.

Thunderdrop Fan
